crime.value: Premeditated stabbing murder of a wife, lured to a secret apartment by a voice impersonation; the question posed to police is who 'Roy Baker' is and where he fled — never that the husband did it
crime.quote: “I’m going to kill you, Carolyn,” he said, and showed her the knife. She died slowly, and noisily.

victim.value: Carolyn Jordan, the suburban wife who was cold to her husband, lived off his salary, and was secretly keeping Village lovers — making her both hated and easily explained as a victim of one of those lovers
victim.quote: It looks as though she was—uh—stepping out on you, Mr. Jordan.

closed_world.value: The double life spanning midtown Manhattan office/alibi hotel, the Christopher Street Village apartment, and the New Hope, Bucks County split-level — a two-identity world only Jordan can cross
closed_world.quote: From that day on he let his two lives overlap.

culprit_and_motive.value: Howard Jordan, adman living as 'Roy Baker,' killed his wife out of hatred for her adultery and for the life she forced on him, using his fabricated identity as the scapegoat
culprit_and_motive.quote: He knew, then, that he hated her, that he had always hated her and, finally, that he was going to do something about it.

resolution.value: No legal resolution — the alibi holds and police hunt a nonexistent man; the ironic punishment is self-inflicted: by killing Carolyn he destroyed Roy Baker and is trapped as Howard Jordan, whom he cannot bear to be
resolution.quote: He had to be Howard Jordan... He simply did not like being Howard Jordan.

investigator.value: The murderer himself as viewpoint character; the nominal investigators are unnamed New York and local police who are wholly deceived
investigator.quote: For form’s sake, the New York police checked Jordan’s whereabouts at the time of the murder

suspect_architecture.value: Minimal/inverted: the reader knows the killer from the start. The only 'suspect' pool is the fictitious Roy Baker (the killer's own alter ego, hunted as a real man), with the folk singer Stud Clement and Carolyn's other Village lovers as ambient alternatives, and the husband Howard Jordan cleared as a matter of form.
suspect_architecture.quote: "Does the name Roy Baker mean anything to you?"

red_herring.value: The manufactured identity itself: Roy Baker, an 'irresponsible Village artist,' is framed as Carolyn's lover-killer, reinforced by an unclaimed airline reservation, abandoned clothes and an untouched bank account suggesting panicked flight.
red_herring.quote: "Baker had made a reservation on a plane shortly after killing Carolyn but hadn't picked up his ticket"

clue_fairness.value: Fully open — the inverted form gives the reader every mechanic in advance: the double wallets, the lease signed in disguised handwriting, the monogrammed suitcase, the hotel-register manipulation and the imitated Tennessee accent are all shown as they are done.
clue_fairness.quote: "he signed it “Roy Baker” in a handwriting quite unlike his own."

social_world.value: Two mutually exclusive class worlds of 1960s New York: Madison Avenue advertising respectability plus Bucks County split-level suburbia, versus the bohemian Village of folksingers, artists and coffee-house chess — with money as the hinge (his salary supports Carolyn, who in turn pays her lover's rent).
social_world.quote: "Jordan, after all, was a square, a Madison Avenue copy chief, an animal of little interest to the folksingers"

alibi.value: A rigged office/hotel alibi: he signs the building register out and in around a sandwich break, leaves unsigned at 6:45 to commit the murder, returns unsigned, departs at 11:15 and sleeps at his habitual hotel where he had reserved a room in advance; police verify it and it holds.
alibi.quote: "they found that he'd been at his office until eleven-fifteen, except for a half hour when he'd had a sandwich"

reveal_mechanic.value: No detective reveal; the demonstration is psychological and self-inflicted — Jordan cannot return to the Village because he would be recognized and arrested as Roy Baker, proving he murdered his own preferred self along with his wife.
reveal_mechanic.quote: "he had killed her—and killed Roy Baker in the bargain, erased him very neatly"

media_and_audience.value: The police narrative packages the crime as a straying suburban wife killed by a shiftless Village bohemian, with the neighbours' gossip supplying the adultery angle and the bereaved-husband role performed for the audience of investigators.
media_and_audience.quote: "A guy like this, he's going to turn up in a certain kind of place. The Village, North Beach in Frisco"

investigator_wound.value: Transferred to the murderer as protagonist: Jordan's wound is that he loathes being Howard Jordan and can only live through an invented self — the crime exploits and then destroys that escape, leaving him trapped in the identity he hates.
investigator_wound.quote: "He simply did not like being Howard Jordan."

victims_enemies.value: Carolyn's only real enemy is her husband Howard Jordan, whose grievance is textured: years of coldness, financial exploitation, his abandoned writing ambitions, and finally her serial infidelity with Village men (Phillie Wells, then Stud Clement, whose rent she paid). Her lovers are transactional, not hostile; the hatred is entirely marital.
victims_enemies.quote: He knew, then, that he hated her, that he had always hated her and, finally, that he was going to do something about it.

suspect_wounds.value: The 'suspect' Roy Baker is wounded by design — a bohemian drifter identity with no verifiable past, a fabricated dead wife, a rented room paid in cash, and an abandoned plane reservation that reads as flight. The real wound is Jordan's own: he cannot inhabit Howard Jordan, and killing Carolyn destroyed the only self he liked.
suspect_wounds.quote: Baker had made a reservation on a plane shortly after killing Carolyn but hadn't picked up his ticket

unreliable_frame.value: Told in close third person aligned wholly with Jordan, who lies to his wife, his landlord, his neighbors, the police and finally rationalizes to himself; his self-analysis ('not blind to its psychological implications') is itself a performance he only sees through at the end.
unreliable_frame.quote: "A mere facade. A con perpetrated upon the soulless bosses."

setting_as_constraint.value: 1960s Manhattan's compartmentalized geography and anonymity: Madison Avenue versus Greenwich Village, separated by a cab ride, lets one man hold two unconnected social worlds. The office sign-in register and the midtown hotel supply a bounded, documentable alibi, while Village indifference means screams go unanswered.
setting_as_constraint.quote: they were in New York now, and New Yorkers never concern themselves with the shrieks of dying women

evidence_type.value: Documentary/testimonial alibi construction — the office signature register, hotel reservation and rumpled bed, plus neighbor testimony about Carolyn's affairs; the corpse is identified by forensic fingerprint records from a prior civil service job.
evidence_type.quote: he'd been at his office until eleven-fifteen, except for a half hour when he'd had a sandwich around the corner

false_suspect.value: Roy Baker — a wholly fictitious Village artist invented by the killer himself, framed by the lease, bank account, wardrobe and abandoned flight booking; police hunt a man who does not exist.
false_suspect.quote: "Does the name Roy Baker mean anything to you?"

technical_detail.value: The mechanics of manufacturing a documented second identity: false name on a lease signed in altered handwriting, cash payment to avoid bank traces, monogrammed suitcase, bank account, book club and mailing-list mail — plus vocal mimicry of Stud Clement's Tennessee accent to lure Carolyn, and the sign-in/sign-out register manipulation.
technical_detail.quote: he signed it "Roy Baker" in a handwriting quite unlike his own.

moral_ambiguity.value: Jordan is a man suffocated by a life he never chose, whose invented self is the only place he is creative, happy and kind; his wife is unfaithful and exploitative. Yet the murder is punished perfectly by its own logic — he destroys the self he loved, and the story ends in existential imprisonment rather than justice.
moral_ambiguity.quote: He simply did not like being Howard Jordan.
